entries.title: follow a symlink to find the package root
entries.body:
`packageRoot()` derived the package from the directory `argv[0]` named and
resolved no symbolic link, so a compiler reached through one looked for
`scripts/build.sh` and `std/` beside the LINK rather than beside the package.
npm links every command that way
(`node_modules/.bin/nish -> ../@amritk/nish/bin/nish`), and so does an admin's
`ln -s /opt/nish/bin/nish /usr/local/bin/nish`.

Measured against the released 0.5.0 compiler, reached through an absolute link
into a staged install: a program importing `nish/text` is refused with ``Module
`nish/text` is not part of the standard library (it has: json, testing, text)``
-- so this is not only a `--link` defect, and it prints the same misleading
sentence the missing-`std/` releases did, for the same reason: the list is a
literal and the file is what the root never reached. A program importing nothing
gets `--link: cannot find scripts/build.sh (looked in <link dir>/.. and .)`,
exit 3. The same binary by its real path compiles both.

The real path of whatever `argv[0]` named is now a candidate for the root, which
is what the `realpathSync` builtin shipped for. Order is where the care is: the
unresolved spelling is tried first, so a compiler that is not reached through a
link answers exactly the root it answered before, spelled the way it was
invoked, and a link is the only thing that adds a candidate at all -- no
ordinary install moves, no golden moves, and the "looked in ..." diagnostic
still names one directory. `argv[0]`'s *spelling* sensitivity (wp19 §A7) is left
alone on purpose: resolving that would move every standard-library path both
compilers print, and it is that bullet's rather than this one's.

The call site waited a release because `self/` compiles under the last RELEASED
compiler, which is the rolling freeze CI's `bootstrap` job checks. Both
installers keep their absolute-path `exec`, now for their own reasons rather
than for this: `install.sh` installs a released compiler that may predate the
fix, and `scripts/postinstall.mjs` execs to take node out from in front of the
compiler. WP21's symlinked-*package* limitation stays declared and its comments
are corrected to say why: the builtin removed the excuse, but package identity
from the real directory and from the manifest answer wp21 §7's diamond
differently, and that is one decision, S3's.

**It carries a second fix, to `nish-cmp` rather than to a compiler.** 0.5.0 gave
that gate the first seed it can use, and the first run against it was red: 4
undeclared differences over 2 programs, all one cause -- a module reached as
`nish/<name>` is resolved against the compiler's own package root and then named
by the path it was found at, so the seed writes its own unpacked path where HEAD
writes `std/text.ts`. Two compilers are never installed in one directory, so
that is a property no run of the tool can compare rather than a difference it
may forgive, and without removing it the gate could not be green for any tree.
`packageRootOf` derives each side's root the way the compilers do and
`withoutOwnRoot` removes it from both sides before the bytes are compared; it is
keyed on no program and no file, it reaches nothing else on those lines,
`selfCheckRoots` drives it over fabricated inputs on every run, and the run
reports what it set aside. The gate's first green run is
`437/437 programs agree (3582 files, 3253862 IR lines) ... 4 equal after each
compiler's own root, 0 undeclared difference(s)`, on both Linux seeds -- which is
the evidence R6 was told to wait for.
metrics: the v0.5.0 seed compiles `self/` with the call site -- `IR(stage1) == IR(stage2)` over 61 modules, `stage3 == stage2` byte-identical; 0 of 2 link spellings worked before, 2 of 2 after; nish-cmp 437/437 against 435/437
tests: tests/run.js wp19 -- an absolute link and npm's relative `.bin` link
each linking then running a program that imports `nish/text`
both watched failing with the fix reverted; and three checks over nish-cmp's own normalisation
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: ask the diagnostic-coverage gate of stage1, not of stage0
entries.body:
WP19 gate G2 reads "every registry code provoked by something that
outlives stage0, or unreachable with a reason", and the number in §5a
that called it closed was measured with stage0 — which does not outlive
stage0. Asked of the compiler R6 leaves behind,
`node tests/diagnostic_coverage.js --compiler build/nish
--require-coverage` answered with 80 findings, each advising the reader
to write a reason that was already written.

**Nothing had been overlooked.** Every one of the 126 programs that
provoke those 80 codes — every program, not merely the first in corpus
order — was already recorded, with the sentence stage1 answers instead,
in `tests/self/parser_refusals.txt` (85 entries),
`tests/wordings/parser_refusals.txt` (39) or `stage1_divergence.txt`
(2). Those registers are per *case* and the criterion is per *code*, and
no file made the step from one to the other. So the tool printed
`(no reason on file)` eighty times for reasons that were on file, and
the gate could only be asked of the compiler R6 deletes.

`tests/wordings/stage0_only.txt` is that step and nothing else: one
`CODE  case[,case...]` line per code, naming programs rather than
repeating sentences, so it cannot drift from the registers without
failing. It is checked from both sides while both compilers exist.
Against stage0 the named set must be **exactly** the set the run found,
so a corpus that grows a case cannot leave a line stale; against stage1
under `--strict-refusals` a code the run provokes fails until its line
is deleted; and every program a line names must be one the corpus has
and one a register declares. A code dropped from the registry, or listed
as unreachable at the same time, fails too. All seven failure modes were
watched firing against a perturbed register before this landed.

`npm test` now passes `--require-coverage` on the stage1 run as well as
the stage0 one, which is what makes the gate's own sentence true of the
compiler that survives. `--report` gains the third state as well: a code
some program provokes that this compiler answers in its parser reads
`stage0 only: <programs> (<register>)` rather than `unreachable: (no
reason on file)`, which was what made a declared parity class look like
a hole in the corpus.

The file empties into `unreachable.txt` at R6, where these wordings
become retired codes because nothing prints them any more.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: pin one diagnostic per declaration when a class body has two bad members
entries.body:
A class whose first field is refused says nothing about its second. `errored`
in `self/context.ts` is set by the first diagnostic and `collectStructMembers`
never clears it between members, so `class Pair { first: i32 = "one"; second:
i32 = "two"; }` names `first` and stops. stage0, the self-hosted compiler and
the released 0.5.0 binary all print that one sentence and all exit 1, so what
was at stake was how complete the diagnostics are, not whether the program is
caught.

That is now a decision with its reasoning next to the code instead of an
accident nobody had written down. `errored` is stage0's `throw` in a language
that has none, and it is cleared exactly where stage0's `catch` is — per
declaration in `self/checker.ts`, per statement in `self/statements.ts`, and
deliberately restored at the one site where stage0 reports and carries on
rather than throwing. `docs/LANGUAGE.md` states the granularity normatively,
pass 1 recovering per declaration, so naming the second member would be a
change to a language rule rather than a bug fix. The reason carries an expiry:
at R6 the compiler this flag imitates is deleted and the granularity becomes
this compiler's own choice.

The alternative was built before being rejected. A stage1 that clears the flag
per member compiles, resurrects no cascade of derived nonsense, and changes the
output of none of the 926 programs in the corpus, so no gate here can see the
difference either way.

`tests/cases/reject_cls_field_init_type_twice` is what stops it drifting in
silence: two classes with two mistyped fields each, so the count is two rather
than four and rather than one. The `.err` pins that count through the `2 errors`
summary line, because a fragment list can require a sentence and cannot forbid
one; under the per-member reset the count is four and the case is red.

`tests/self/goldens/checked_self.txt` moves because the explanation adds lines
to `self/structs.ts` and the checked dump records line:column; it was
regenerated from stage1, seeded with the released 0.5.0 binary, which
re-checked the rolling freeze in the same run.
metrics: 926 corpus programs compiled by both stage1 binaries, 0 differ with the per-member reset applied
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: port the three ELF-assuming checks that keep macos-latest out of the test matrix
entries.body:
Three checks in `tests/run.js` asserted an ELF fact about a linked binary
rather than the property they exist for, so each failed on a mac without
anything being wrong with the compiler.

Two read `.debug_line` out of the executable. On Mach-O that section is empty
by design: `clang -g` leaves the DWARF in the object files and the executable
keeps only a debug map naming them, and the Darwin driver runs `dsymutil` at
the end of a compile-and-link to turn that map into a `.dSYM` bundle.
`lineTableOf` answers with the file the platform actually used, and both
checks assert what they always asserted about it: the table names
`dbg_main.ts` and has at least one row. Running `dsymutil` afterwards is
deliberately not a fallback — by then clang has deleted the objects the map
names, and the tool writes an empty table and exits 0.

The third asserted that a `--threads` module *refuses to link* against a
runtime built without `-DNISH_THREADS`. That is ELF's rule about a TLS
reference to a non-TLS definition, and ld64 does not have it: measured on
`macos-latest`, clang exits 0, `nm -m` shows `_nish_arena` as a plain
`(__DATA,__common)` symbol where a thread-local descriptor should be, and the
binary segfaults on its first allocation while the matched build of the same
inputs prints `alloc_smoke delta = 16` and exits 0. The property both
platforms can be held to is therefore not the link error but that the
mismatch is never quietly a working-looking program with two arenas, and the
check's name says which mechanism caught it.

The `macos-latest` row stays out of the matrix, because a re-run with these
three ported reports six other failures in three causes. The comment beside
`os:` and the CI matrix section of `docs/wp10-ci.md` now name those six with
the run that measured them, and both drop the claim that nothing in the file
runs on macOS: the darwin pair's `attachedSince` is 0.4.0, so `bootstrap
(aarch64-darwin)` and `bootstrap (x86_64-darwin)` have been green for two
releases.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: measure the `-o dir/` stem collision, which both compilers have
entries.body:
WP19 §A7 recorded that stage1 writes one `.ll` where stage0 writes two when
two modules share a `; ModuleID` under `-o <dir>/`, and filed it as stage1's
own defect, older than the change that found it and unmeasured by anything.
Measured now, the row is wrong in both of its halves, and what is underneath
it is worse than what it described.

The mechanism cannot happen. A stage1 module's name *is* the path string it
was opened at, and `Compilation.byPath` is keyed on that same string, so two
modules never share a name: a duplicate name is a duplicate identity and is
deduplicated at load rather than mis-written at emit. Only stage0, which keeps
the identity and the name in two fields, can hold two different files under
one `; ModuleID`. That is also what every earlier attempt at a reproduction
ran into, and it was written down one file away the whole time, in
`resolvePath`'s comment in `self/paths.ts`.

The outcome does happen, and to both compilers, because `outputStems` drops
every `.` and `..` segment of the entry-relative path before joining it — so a
module above the entry's directory collapses onto one below it with the same
tail and the second overwrites the first. Two relative imports are enough:
`./lib/util` and `../lib/util` from `src/main.ts` writes `out/lib_util.ll`
twice and leaves `out/main.ll` calling a function that no `.ll` in the
directory defines. Through `--link` a user meets it as `ld.lld: error:
duplicate symbol` on a symbol their program defines exactly once. The two
compilers agree byte for byte while doing it, which is why no parity gate has
ever seen it — and once the entry's spelling varies both directions are
reachable, including stage0 dropping a module where stage1 keeps it.

Nothing is fixed here, on purpose. The two `outputStems` are one lowering in
two files, so a one-sided fix would turn a shared bug into a parity
difference, and the fix moves a stem that is live. §5a item 5 carries the four
invocations, their measurements and what a fix takes.

The disambiguating branch turned out to have no coverage at all — every
`tests/link/` program reaches modules whose basenames are already unique, so
the fallback is never taken. `tests/link/module_stem_clash` takes it: two
`text.ts` in one program, answering `a_text` and `b_text`, with a line of
`expected.ir` from each module, so a regression that collided them drops one
from the emitted set rather than merely misnaming it. It reaches no package on
purpose, because a package module's stem is reached by climbing out to
wherever the compiler is installed: such a program writes a different file
name under every install, and `tests/nish-cmp.js` pairs the two compilers'
outputs by file name, so it could never be green on the G2 gate — which is one
more reason the fix is worth making.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: name a package module by its package-relative specifier, in both compilers
entries.body:
A module imported as `nish/<name>` is resolved against the compiler's own
package root — `<dirname(argv[0])>/..` — and stage1 then *named* it by the path
it was found at, so one program's IR was a fact about the install rather than
about the program:

```
./build/nish prog.ts -o out/        ; ModuleID = 'std/text.ts'
/abs/build/nish prog.ts -o out/     ; ModuleID = '/abs/.../std/text.ts'
```

Two installs of one compiler gave one program a different `; ModuleID`, a
different `source_filename` and different `DIFile` paths. The harness happened
to invoke the spelling that agreed, which is the whole reason this family read
as closed (`docs/wp19-stage0-retirement.md` §A7's third bullet).

A package module's **identity** is still the path it was opened at — a file has
to be opened — and its **name** is now its package-relative specifier,
`std/text.ts`, on both sides: `ModuleUnit.name` in `self/compilation.ts` carries
it and `SourceFile` is built from it, so the IR header, the `DIFile`, the
diagnostics, the interop sidecars and the no-`-o` output path all read one
string that no install can move. stage0 already answered that for `nish/` and
needed no naming change; what it gains here is the language rule underneath it.
"Package-relative" had been a description of the specifiers people write rather
than a property of the name — `nish/../../escape/lib` resolved if a file
happened to sit there, and was then named from wherever the compiler was
installed. Both compilers refuse it now, in the same sentence and at the same
span, so no segment of a `nish/` specifier may be empty or begin with a `.`.

A bare-specifier package needed no move, and that was measured rather than
assumed: `findPackageDir` walks up from the importing module's own name and
never asks `packageRoot()`, so `tests/link/package_bare` names its modules
`node_modules/pkg_bare/src/index.ts` under every spelling of `argv[0]` and
identically in both compilers. The standard library was the exception because it
alone resolves against the compiler's install.

**What a released seed now reports through `nish-cmp`, and why this is a decided
output change.** The gate's summary carries `4 equal after each compiler's own
root`: the v0.5.0 seed writes `<unpack path>/std/text.ts` where HEAD writes
`std/text.ts`, and `withoutOwnRoot` removes each compiler's own root
symmetrically so the two compare equal. That was a prediction and this
repository has five recorded instances of a prediction about a gate being wrong,
so it was run: `438/438 programs agree … 4 equal after each compiler's own root,
0 undeclared difference(s)`, before this change and after it, with the same four
files. Nothing moves while the seed predates the fix. Once a release carrying it
is the seed, those four files are equal *as they stand* and that count goes to
0 — which a reader should take as the normalisation having nothing left to do
rather than as four files having stopped being compared, because every byte of
them is compared either way. The output change behind it is the intended one: a
standard-library module's IR is now byte-identical between two installs of one
compiler, measured on two staged installs.

Two consequences, both of them stage1 moving onto stage0's answer. With no `-o`
at all, stage1 wrote the module into its own installation —
`<install>/std/text.ll`, which is `EACCES` under a root-owned install and a
silent edit of the compiler's tree otherwise — and writes `std/text.ll` under
the user's working directory now. And stage1 can now hold two modules under one
`; ModuleID`, exactly as stage0 can, because the name is no longer the identity;
`byPath` is still keyed on the identity, so they are still two modules and still
two files. `outputStems` is deliberately untouched on both sides, so a package
module's output *stem* still climbs out to the install: one program writes
`…_install-a_std_text.ll` and `…_install-b_std_text.ll` from two installs whose
IR for that module is byte-identical. That is the two-sided fix §5a item 5
carries, and a package-relative name is what makes it a small one.
metrics: nish-cmp 438/438 programs, 4 equal after each compiler's own root, before and after; three spellings of argv[0] agree on one `; ModuleID`; IR(stage1) == IR(stage2) over 61 modules and stage3 == stage2 against the v0.5.0 seed
tests: tests/run.js ("a nish/<module> is named package-relatively under every spelling of argv[0]")
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: re-derive G1 on the deletion head, and tally the nish-cmp cycle
entries.body:
Two rows of §5a carried a measurement taken on `862c7cc` on 2026-09-19, and
four pull requests have landed since. A row that states a number without
re-deriving it is the pathology this document has recorded five times, so both
are re-derived here rather than re-asserted.

**G1, on the head R6's deletion would land on.** `node tests/run.js --parity`
on merged `main` at `3927242`: `parity: 14544 runs over 909 programs
(2663.3 s); 0 undeclared difference(s), 2808 declared`, exit 0. The deltas
against the 2026-09-19 row decompose rather than needing to be trusted: seven
entry programs arrived between the two runs — `io_realpath`,
`reject_realpath_arity`, `reject_realpath_type`, `builtin_realpath`,
`reject_cls_field_init_type_twice`, `reject_std_escaping_module` and
`module_stem_clash/main.ts`, whose two imported `text.ts` are modules rather
than programs — and seven programs across the sixteen variations is exactly the
112 new runs. The ten new declared rows are those programs meeting declaration
classes that already existed; no `DECLARED` entry names any of them, which is
the difference between a corpus that grew and a gate that was widened.

**G2.1 as a cycle rather than as one run.** Item 1 said the deletion should
rest on the `nish-cmp` runs nobody arranged, and twelve of them now exist: two
architectures across six `ci.yml` runs on `main` since 2026-09-21. No red row,
and every row that printed a summary reports `4 equal after each compiler's own
root` and `0 undeclared difference(s)`. That the normalisation count has not
moved off 4 is the part worth reading: `withoutOwnRoot` was allowed into the
gate on the ground that it is keyed on no program and no file, so a fifth
normalised file would be the gate forgiving more than was argued for it, and a
tally is how that is noticed instead of assumed. #136 is the case in point — it
changed how a package module is named, predicted the count would stay at 4
while the seed predates the fix, and CI agreed to the byte on both rows.

Two of the twelve are `cancelled` rather than green, and the cause is this
workflow rather than the gate: `cancel-in-progress: true` killed run 614 when
#135's merge arrived fifty-one seconds after #133's. Nothing is unproven by it,
but a green-row tally on `main` has a hole wherever two merges land inside a
minute, and that is written down so the next reader does not have to rediscover
it.

Item 3 is restated as what it now is. Three of its checks are ported and assert
one property on both object formats (#133); six remain red, named with the run
that measured them, and the `LC_UUID` cause behind three of those is settled —
ld64 varies it with the output path, so a comparison that links two copies of
one input to two paths fails at identical size. The row is still out of the
matrix, so this item stays open. The claim that nothing in the file runs on
macOS is gone from here as well as from `ci.yml`: the darwin `bootstrap` rows
have been green for two releases, and they are where the `LC_UUID` finding came
from.

`.claude/selfhost.md`'s R1 row carried the same stale number and is re-derived
with it. Its standing qualification gains the sharper example: `outputStems` is
a defect both compilers have, which no parity run can ever see, because the two
agree byte for byte while committing it.
metrics: parity 14544 runs over 909 programs, 0 undeclared, 2808 declared, exit 0, on 3927242; twelve nish-cmp rows on main since 2026-09-21, 0 red, 4 equal after each compiler's own root throughout
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: refuse on a platform with no prebuilt compiler instead of falling back to Node
entries.body:
`bin/nish` was `import "../dist/launcher.js"`, so the shipped package's entry
point was itself built from `src/` — and WP19 R6 deletes `src/`. The launcher
and its packaging helper are now plain ESM under `bin/`, needing no build step,
and `package.json` no longer ships `dist`.

That removes the Node fallback, which is a decided output change rather than a
consequence nobody weighed. A platform with no prebuilt binary is refused with
a diagnostic naming all four supported targets, the package npm should have
installed, and a remedy, and it exits 3; under `--json` it is one object on
stdout carrying `NL0002`, the code the registry already defines for a toolchain
that could not be run. musl, FreeBSD and every 32-bit platform lose
`npm install`, which `docs/wp19-stage0-retirement.md` §6 records as a cost of
retirement rather than leaving to be discovered.

Nothing is compiled on a user's machine on any path, which is what the
installer was for; supported platforms still download and unpack.
metrics: the tarball goes 588,943 bytes / 179 files to 160,817 / 35, both packed the same way from clean checkouts. That is the tarball and not the install — node_modules/typescript is 23,452 KiB, and removing that dependency is R6's.
tests: npm pack and npm install rather than copying files into node_modules
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: let the unsigned widths cross as arrays
entries.body:
`u8[]`, `u16[]`, `u32[]` and `u64[]` now reach a host as `Uint8Array`,
`Uint16Array`, `Uint32Array` and `BigUint64Array`, across the wasm loader and
the N-API shim (WP30, `docs/wp30-bytes-interop.md`). The package is four rows
in `typedView` plus `elemSize` widening to `1 | 2 | 4 | 8`, because the scoping
found the rest already existed: the language has `u8[]` and lowers it like
every other array, `nish_alloc_array(1, n)` is a byte buffer the runtime
already makes, the generated loader already takes `elemSize` as an argument,
and both N-API helpers already take the typed-array tag and the element size.
One row produces the declaration, the loader entry and the C header's element
comment together.

An array of an unsigned width needs none of the masking its scalar twin needs,
and that is what the tests pin. A scalar `u32` result travels in an i32 value
type and reaches JavaScript negative above 2^31 unless the loader restores it;
an element never travels in a value type at all -- it is a byte in `data` that
`Uint32Array` reads unsigned, and a store through one truncates exactly as the
language wraps, so a mask there would be wrong rather than redundant.
`fillU8(xs: u8[], v: u8)` puts both rules in one generated call: `arrayIn`
hands the array over untouched, `v & 0xff` masks the scalar, and `copyBack`
returns the arena bytes because the fixpoint proved the callee writes through.

The new rows exposed a wrong indefinite article. `withArticle` and the
generated loader's `TypeError` both tested `/^[AEIOU]/`, so a host read `must
be an Uint8Array`; the rule had held by accident while `Int32Array` was the
only vowel-initial constructor in the table. `u` is out of the set now in all
four places, because the article follows the vowel sound.

`docs/LANGUAGE.md` said there was "no `Uint8Array` / `Float32Array`", which was
already wrong about `Float32Array` and became misleading about `Uint8Array`.
The alias names are exactly four, an unsigned array has none, and that
asymmetry is a spelling rather than a capability.

`cmpSince` moves 0.5.0 -> 0.6.0, so `nish-cmp` (WP19 G2.1) gets no row until
0.6.0 ships. WP30 changes generated output on purpose, so HEAD and the 0.5.0
seed disagree about eleven files -- eight loaders sharing the article line, and
three sidecars of `bench/scan.ts` where 0.5.0 declines a `u8[]` HEAD exports.
`DECLARED` cannot cover them because it wants words in a `CHANGELOG.md`
generated at release time; reverting the article fix reaches green on none of
the three that are the feature; and keeping `bench/scan.ts` out of the corpus
would go green by arranging for the comparison not to see the change. An absent
row says the true thing instead. The cost is in the field's note: G2.1 is dark
for every change until 0.6.0, so an unintended output change in that window is
caught by nothing. It rides in this change rather than following it because
`release.yml`'s `release` job is `needs: ci` -- a red `main` cuts no release,
and only a release carrying WP30 clears the difference.

Also here: `bench/scan.ts`, `web/bytes-worker.mjs` and `bench/worker.mjs`,
which measured the worker boundary. An empty worker round trip is ~61 us
against ~0.8 us of work, so a worker answering one document per message is
~99% `postMessage`; the worker takes a list and exports `scanBatch` for callers
below the break-even of ~74 documents or ~12 KB.
metrics: 17/17 programs agree, 85 sidecars, 470104 bytes byte-identical between stage0 and stage1; u32 element 4294967295 not -1, u64 element 2^63+1 positive, u8 elements 200 and 255 unsigned; JSON.parse 1.6 us against 0.8 us to copy and scan the same 164 bytes
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: freeze the WP13 differential rewrite as goldens, with a staleness guard
entries.body:
§2B listed the WP13 differential suite as surviving R6 and it does not: the
comparison needs no second *compiler*, but the JavaScript it compares against is
typed by stage0's own `Compilation`, which `tests/differential/rewrite.js`
drives in process because `i32`, `u8`, `f32` and `i64` are all just `number` to
`tsc`'s checker. Deleting `src/` would take the reference generator with it, and
this is the only oracle in the repository about **runtime semantics** rather
than emitted text.

So the reference is frozen while stage0 exists (G2.4).
`tests/differential/goldens/rewrites.txt` holds the rewritten `.mjs` of all 176
programs — 358 modules, 354 distinct bodies, 235 KiB — and
`tests/differential/run.js --frozen` runs the comparison from it, automatically
when there is no rewriter to load. Neither half of the harness names stage0 any
more: the native side takes `--compiler` or the seed protocol's answer.
Measured, the freeze costs nothing it was meant to keep: `164/176 programs agree
with Node` from the live rewriter and `164/176` from the store, the same 176
verdicts in the same order.

The staleness guard is the engineering content. Each record carries the SHA-256
of the bytes of every module the program loads and its `.args` verbatim, so a
program whose source has moved fails as `STALE` — ahead of
`known-failures.txt`, which records decisions about the language and not
references that have rotted. `goldens.js` rebuilds the whole store from the live
rewriter and requires byte equality, which is the only form that leaves no
column uncompared; freshness alone survives R6 and asks four questions rather
than one. It fired for real while the branch was open: #138 landed a corpus
program with an entry point, and the verify said `175/176 programs fresh, the
store differs from the live rewrite` instead of comparing the 175 it held.

What could not be frozen is priced in §6 as the sixth cost rather than left to
be discovered: the fuzz differential against Node, whose programs come from a
seed and so have no reference to freeze; `arrow-parity.js`, whose subject *is*
the rewriter; the store's own fidelity half; and every corpus program added
after R6, which gets no differential coverage until somebody ports the rewrite
onto stage1's `--emit-checked` dump. One finding is recorded with it: pointing
the native half at the seed stops two corpus programs compiling, on `-1 / z`
with `z: f64`, and the reason no gate saw it is that `CORPUS_DIRS` does not
include `tests/differential/corpus`.
metrics: 164/176 live and 164/176 frozen, verdict-identical row by row

entries.title: type a signed or parenthesised numeric literal from the other operand
entries.body:
`docs/LANGUAGE.md` says a numeric literal takes the type of the other operand
of a binary operator, and that "`-5` and `(5)` count as the literal". stage1
matched only the bare spelling on the left-hand side, so `-1 / z` with
`z: f64` was refused with ``Operator `/` requires two operands of the same
numeric type, got i32 and f64`` on a program stage0 compiles. The reach was
wider than the sign: `(1) / z` was refused identically, because
`checkOperator` in `self/expressions.ts` tested `leftNode.kind === N_NUMBER`
and both `N_UNARY` and `N_PAREN` are nodes in their own right. It held for
every operator, against every typed right operand — a variable, a field, an
element, a user call, a conversion call — and for `f64`, `f32` and `i64`
alike. The right-hand side was never affected, because the wanted type is
threaded into it either way: `z / -1` has always worked. `literalOperand`
unwraps the two spellings, which is the same list `peekable` walks and the
same list stage0's `contextType` climbs out of.

It was found by compiling `tests/differential/corpus` with stage1 for the
first time, and the reason that was the first time is the larger half of this
change. `CORPUS_DIRS` in `tests/self/corpus.js` did not name that directory,
so its 71 whole programs — WP13's differential set, the one corpus here built
to hold a compiled program's behaviour against the same program run under Node
— were compiled by stage1 by no oracle, by `goldens.js`, by `nish-cmp.js` or
under any of `--parity`'s sixteen variations. `.claude/selfhost.md` listed the
directory as part of the corpus and `scripts/arrow-verify.mjs` carried a
private enumerator whose header said the opposite. The directory is in
`CORPUS_DIRS` now, `programs()` counts a subdirectory holding a `main.ts` as
one program — which brings in the three multi-module differential programs and
`examples/multi/`, absent for as long as it has existed — and the private
enumerator is gone, so there is one rule again.

Two of the 71 were the compile errors above; the other 69 agreed byte for byte
on their IR and on their `--emit-checked` dump before any fix.
`checked_oracle.js` would not have failed on the two: it printed `N rejected by
stage1` and exited 0. It fails now, and prints the rejection whether or not
`--verbose` was asked for; both oracles were watched exiting 1 on the two
programs with the checker fix reverted.

`docs/wp19-stage0-retirement.md` gains §A9, the sixth entry in §A5's series of
occasions on which a green gate meant less than it looked — the first that is
about the corpus's own definition rather than about a stale measurement or an
unwritten variation. G1's standing qualification gains a second clause: the
difference set is a lower bound over the corpus somebody enumerated as well as
over the programs and the variations somebody wrote. The G1 rows in §3, §5 and
§5a and `.claude/selfhost.md`'s R1 row now say which corpus their number
covered, because the cross product is 986 programs where that number was 909,
and the full re-derivation is named as owed rather than guessed at. §6 item 6,
which #141 wrote from the differential side, records that both halves of its
finding are closed.
metrics: 71/71 programs agree on IR and on the checked dump, against 69/69 with 2 rejected by stage1 before; parity 1136 runs over 71 programs, 0 undeclared, 142 declared, every declaration a class that already existed; npm test 2177 passed, 0 failed, 2 skipped
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: pay the parity figure §A9 left owed, over the whole 986-program corpus
entries.body:
§A9 put `tests/differential/corpus` and the directory programs into
`CORPUS_DIRS`, taking the cross product from 909 programs to 986. It wrote
every row that quoted the old number to say which corpus it had covered, and
left the full figure explicitly owed rather than guessed at. This pays it:

    parity: 15776 runs over 986 programs (2938.5 s); 0 undeclared difference(s), 2961 declared

exit 0, on merged `main` at 1e95aac, from `node tests/run.js --parity` — zero
undeclared over the widened corpus, including the 71 programs no parity run had
ever touched.

It took three attempts and only the third is quoted. The first was killed when
`main` moved under it, which is §A7's own lesson about a number with a one-day
shelf life; the second was SIGTERMed by a neighbour on a shared four-core box at
load 13; the third ran on an idle box with `npm ci` and `npm run build` chained
before the mode so they could not overlap, because a parity run overlapping a
rebuild once reported 749 undeclared differences where the same run alone
reported 0. A run that prints no summary line says nothing, and neither of the
first two printed one.

The declared count moved 2808 to 2961, and that delta is left undecomposed on
purpose. 142 of the 153 are §A9's 74 programs meeting declaration classes that
already existed; the remaining 11 belong to the `multi` selection and to the
programs WP30 brought. Attributing them needs the mode's own program set rather
than the corpus module's — `parity.js` counts 986 where `programs()` and
`linkPrograms()` enumerate 538, because the mode compares refusals too — and
deriving a breakdown from the wrong set is how this paragraph would have stated
something false.

The G1 rows in §3, §5 and §5a and R1 in `.claude/selfhost.md` carry the new
figure and name the head it was taken on; the corpus-growth series gains its
eighth term.
metrics: parity 15776 runs over 986 programs, 0 undeclared, 2961 declared, exit 0, on 1e95aac at load 0.24
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon
